> 「可以身相见如来不？」「不也，世尊！不可以身相得见如来。何以故？如来所说身相，即非身相。」佛告须菩提：「凡所有相，皆是虚妄。若见诸相非相，即见如来。」

Five sections in, the sutra asks the question that most religious practice is built on: can you see the teacher?

Not "can you meet him" in the ordinary sense. Can the Awakened One be recognised by appearance — by the body, the marks, the radiance, the signs that tradition says a buddha carries?

The answer is no, and the reason given is the formula that will recur thirty-odd times before the sutra ends: 如来所说身相，即非身相. What is called the body of a buddha is not the body of a buddha — therefore it is called the body of a buddha.

## 身相 is appearance as evidence

相 is not "appearance" in the weak sense of looks. It is the mark by which something is identified and certified. The thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks are, in the old idiom, a credential: this is what a buddha looks like, this is how you know one when you see one.

So the question is evidentiary. And the answer removes the credential from the domain of evidence.

## 虚妄 does not mean unreal

The most damaging misreading of this section is also the most popular one: *all appearances are illusory, so nothing matters, nothing is there.*

虚妄 in this vocabulary means: without a permanent, independent, self-existing substance. It does not mean absent. It means dependent, impermanent, unable to serve as a final ground.

The distinction matters because it decides how you live. If appearances were nothing, you could walk through walls and ignore the person in front of you. If appearances are conditional arisings, they function fully — and precisely because they function, you cannot treat them as final.

## 若见诸相非相 is not blurring your eyes

The instruction is not to stop seeing. It is to see clearly and to stop gripping.

The book's phrasing: see the mark, know it as a conditional appearance, and do not climb onto it. The image stays sharp. What drops away is the worship — the small, automatic promotion of a thing into a ground.

Applied to the Buddha's body, this is the sharpest case available: the most sacred object in the tradition is subjected to the same rule as everything else.

## Which leaves the statue question

Does this mean images are to be avoided? The book's answer is practical rather than polemical. Bowing to a statue, visualising a figure, is an expedient — it gathers the mind and produces reverence. The error is not in the statue; it is in the assumption that the statue *is* the thing.

Expedients are usable. They are not holdable. That is the whole distinction between 方便 and 执相.

## 即见如来

The sentence ends with what sounds like a promise: see marks as non-marks, and you see the Tathāgata.

But the Tathāgata is 如 — *thus*. 如者真如，来者显现: appearing as it actually is. There is no separate being to be glimpsed at the end of this sentence. What appears, when the marks are no longer treated as grounds, is the way things are.

This is why the phrase is 即见 and not 当见 — *then* you see, not *later* you will see. It is not a future attainment.

## The test

Take the most impressive thing you know. A person you admire, a work you consider great, an experience you call profound. Look at it directly.

Then ask what you are using it for. Are you looking at it, or are you leaning on it to certify something about yourself?

The difference is the entire content of this section, and it is usually easier to see in the impressive case than in the ordinary ones.
